claim: Prolonged activity deprivation can lead to rebound hyperactivity and seizures.
source: Prolonged activity deprivation can lead to rebound hyperactivity and seizures.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citation in this sentence, though it is supported by citations elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: In cortical slice cultures made from knockout mice lacking all three PARbZIP factors, the network response to prolonged activity withdrawal measured with calcium imaging is much stronger, while baseline activity is unchanged.
source: In cortical slice cultures made from knockout mice lacking all three of these factors, the network response to prolonged activity withdrawal measured with calcium imaging is much stronger, while baseline activity is unchanged.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2 showing calcium imaging measurements comparing WT and TKO slices.

claim: Whole-cell recordings reveal an exaggerated increase in the frequency of miniature excitatory synaptic currents reflecting enhanced upregulation of recurrent excitatory synaptic transmission in TKO mice.
source: Whole-cell recordings reveal an exaggerated increase in the frequency of miniature excitatory synaptic currents reflecting enhanced upregulation of recurrent excitatory synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3 showing mEPSC measurements.

claim: Two of the PARbZIP factors, Hlf and Tef, are critical for constraining plasticity and for preventing life-threatening seizures.
source: Genetic analyses reveal that two of the factors, Hlf and Tef, are critical for constraining plasticity and for preventing life-threatening seizures.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic analysis data presented in Figure 6 and Figure 7 showing the effects of different allele combinations on plasticity and survival.

claim: Transcriptional activation is not only required for many forms of homeostatic plasticity but is also involved in restraint of the response to activity deprivation.
source: These data indicate that transcriptional activation is not only required for many forms of homeostatic plasticity but is also involved in restraint of the response to activity deprivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity can alter the intrinsic excitability of individual neurons, as well as the strength and number of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: Homeostatic plasticity can alter the intrinsic excitability of individual neurons, as well as the strength and number of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses (Davis, 2006; Turrigiano and Nelson, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Synaptic changes can occur post- or presynaptically and may scale quantal amplitudes and alter the frequency of quantal events.
source: Synaptic changes can occur post- (Turrigiano et al., 1998) or presynaptically (Delvendahl and Müller, 2019) and may scale quantal amplitudes and alter the frequency of quantal events.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Homeostatic mechanisms are strong during development and can be maladaptive if they overshoot or are activated inappropriately.
source: Especially during development, homeostatic mechanisms are strong and can be maladaptive if they overshoot or are activated inappropriately (Nelson and Valakh, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Whether and how the strength of homeostatic plasticity is normally constrained has remained unknown.
source: Despite recognition of the significance of homeostatic plasticity, whether and how its strength is normally constrained has remained unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Negative regulators of homeostatic plasticity have not been previously described.
source: However, such negative regulators of homeostatic plasticity have not been previously described.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The PAR bZIP family consists of hepatic leukemia factor (HLF), thyrotroph embryonic factor (TEF), and albumin D-site-binding protein (DBP) which are thought to act as transcriptional activators, as well as E4 Promoter-Binding Protein 4 (E4BP4, currently known as Nfil3) that acts as a transcriptional repressor.
source: The family consists of hepatic leukemia factor (HLF), thyrotroph embryonic factor (TEF), and albumin D-site-binding protein (DBP) which are thought to act as transcriptional activators, as well as E4 Promoter-Binding Protein 4 (E4BP4, currently known as Nfil3) that acts as a transcriptional repressor (Mitsui et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: All four PAR bZIP family members share the same DNA binding motif.
source: All four family members share the same DNA binding motif.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the PAR bZIP family.

claim: DBP is a circadian gene controlled by CLOCK and oscillates with circadian rhythm.
source: DBP is a circadian gene controlled by CLOCK and oscillates with circadian rhythm (Ripperger et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Other PAR bZIP family members are also controlled by CLOCK.
source: Other family members are also controlled by CLOCK (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: While PAR bZIP TFs typically have oscillatory behavior in peripheral tissue, they do not oscillate in the brain outside of the SCN.
source: However, while these TFs typically have oscillatory behavior in peripheral tissue, they do not oscillate in the brain outside of the SCN (Gachon et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Loss of HLF, TEF, and DBP has been associated with epilepsy.
source: Loss of HLF, TEF, and DBP has been associated with epilepsy (Gachon et al., 2004; Hawkins and Kearney, 2016; Rambousek et al., 2020) suggesting they are important in regulating network activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Prolonged activity deprivation activates a robust transcriptional program involving the PARbZIP TF family members HLF and TEF.
source: In order to investigate the role that gene transcription plays in regulating the neuronal response to activity deprivation, we profiled changes in gene expression engaged during homeostatic plasticity and found that prolonged activity deprivation activates a robust transcriptional program involving the PARbZIP TF family members HLF and TEF.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1.

claim: HLF and TEF act to restrain the expression of homeostatic plasticity.
source: Both act to restrain the expression of homeostatic plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing exaggerated homeostatic responses in TKO mice.

claim: HLF and TEF have limited effects on network function at baseline.
source: While they have limited effects on network function at baseline, they strongly suppress the upregulation of homeostatic changes, mainly by regulating recurrent excitatory synaptic connections, although inhibition is also affected.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging and electrophysiology data showing no difference in baseline activity but exaggerated responses to TTX.

claim: HLF and TEF strongly suppress the upregulation of homeostatic changes, mainly by regulating recurrent excitatory synaptic connections, although inhibition is also affected.
source: While they have limited effects on network function at baseline, they strongly suppress the upregulation of homeostatic changes, mainly by regulating recurrent excitatory synaptic connections, although inhibition is also affected.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data showing effects on mEPSCs and mIPSCs.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity is itself subject to activity-dependent regulation and is transcriptionally restrained by the PARbZIP TFs HLF and TEF.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that homeostatic plasticity is itself subject to activity-dependent regulation and is transcriptionally restrained by the PARbZIP TFs HLF and TEF.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Certain forms of homeostatic plasticity require transcription.
source: Certain forms of homeostatic plasticity require transcription (Goold and Nicoll, 2010; Ibata et al., 2008) and activity perturbation results in changes in gene expression (Schaukowitch et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activity perturbation results in changes in gene expression.
source: Certain forms of homeostatic plasticity require transcription (Goold and Nicoll, 2010; Ibata et al., 2008) and activity perturbation results in changes in gene expression (Schaukowitch et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Organotypic slice cultures cut at P7 and cultured for 5 days reform connections and spontaneous bouts of activity termed upstates emerge.
source: We cut coronal slices including neocortex at P7 and cultured them for 5 days. During this culture period, the neurons reform connections, and spontaneous bouts of activity, termed upstates, emerge (Johnson and Buonomano, 2007; Koch et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing the slice culture system.

claim: TTX (0.5 μM) applied for 5 days during an early developmental period (equivalent postnatal days, EP, 12–17) induces a robust homeostatic program and profoundly changes network dynamics.
source: To broadly block activity, we applied the voltage-gated sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin, TTX (0.5 μM), for 5 days during an early developmental period (equivalent postnatal days, EP, 12–17). This manipulation induces a robust homeostatic program and profoundly changes network dynamics (Koch et al., 2010; Schaukowitch et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and by the experimental data in the current study.

claim: Inactivity activates a robust transcriptional program of both positively and negatively affected genes consistent with data from dissociated hippocampal cultures.
source: Inactivity activates a robust transcriptional program of both positively and negatively affected genes (Figure 1A) consistent with data from dissociated hippocampal cultures (Schaukowitch et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A and by citation to prior literature.

claim: The most overrepresented subfamily among TFs differentially expressed during activity blockade was the PARbZIP subfamily of TFs.
source: We asked which families or subfamilies were most overrepresented among the TFs differentially expressed during activity blockade. The most overrepresented subfamily or family was the PARbZIP subfamily of TFs, a subtype of the CEBP-related family in the class of Basic leucine zipper factors (classification data from tfclass.bioinf.med.uni-goettingen.de; Wingender et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data and citation to the TF classification database.

claim: Expression levels of Dbp are much lower than those of Hlf and Tef (<3 TPM in excitatory and PV+ inhibitory neurons).
source: Expression levels of Dbp are much lower than those of Hlf and Tef (<3 TPM in excitatory and PV+ inhibitory neurons), suggesting that this family member may play a more limited role in the neocortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Both Hlf and Tef are robustly upregulated after 5 days of activity deprivation in both excitatory neurons (fold change [FC] TTX/control; FC = 2.6, 2.5; adjusted p value; padj = 1.3e−8, 3.8e−4) and inhibitory neurons (FC = 7.0, 2.1; padj = 4.6e−39, 2.0e−3).
source: Both Hlf and Tef are robustly upregulated after 5 days of activity deprivation in both excitatory (fold change [FC] TTX/control; FC = 2.6, 2.5; adjusted p value; padj = 1.3e−8, 3.8e−4,) and inhibitory neurons (FC = 7.0, 2.1; padj = 4.6e−39, 2.0e−3), while Nfil3 and Dbp were not (FC = 0.51, 1.9; padj = 0.49, 0.80, excitatory; FC = 1.2, 1.4; padj = 0.84, 0.79 inhibitory).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data with statistical analysis.

claim: Nfil3 and Dbp were not significantly upregulated after 5 days of activity deprivation (FC = 0.51, 1.9; padj = 0.49, 0.80, excitatory; FC = 1.2, 1.4; padj = 0.84, 0.79 inhibitory).
source: Both Hlf and Tef are robustly upregulated after 5 days of activity deprivation in both excitatory (fold change [FC] TTX/control; FC = 2.6, 2.5; adjusted p value; padj = 1.3e−8, 3.8e−4,) and inhibitory neurons (FC = 7.0, 2.1; padj = 4.6e−39, 2.0e−3), while Nfil3 and Dbp were not (FC = 0.51, 1.9; padj = 0.49, 0.80, excitatory; FC = 1.2, 1.4; padj = 0.84, 0.79 inhibitory).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data with statistical analysis.

claim: Upregulation of Hlf and Tef occurs soon after activity withdrawal, since by 4 hr of TTX application the level of both TFs is already substantially elevated.
source: We find that upregulation occurs soon after activity withdrawal, since by 4 hr of TTX application the level of both TFs is already substantially elevated (Figure 1C), consistent with previous findings in dissociated hippocampal cultures (Schaukowitch et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C and by citation to prior literature.

claim: Hlf and Tef continue to increase with time, suggesting that their upregulation correlates with how long the network has been silenced.
source: We also find that Hlf and Tef continue to increase with time, suggesting that their upregulation correlates with how long the network has been silenced.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data and represents an inference about the correlation.

claim: Triple knockout (TKO) Hlf−/−/Dbp−/−/Tef−/− mice have epilepsy.
source: Specifically, triple knockout (TKO) Hlf−/−/Dbp−/−/Tef−/− mice have epilepsy (Gachon et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: After 2 days of TTX treatment, the frequency of upstates increases 3.6-fold in wild-type (WT) slices (from 0.06 ± 0.01 to 0.22 ± 0.04 Hz).
source: While 2 days of TTX incubation increases the peak frequency 3.6-fold in wild-type (WT) slices (from 0.06 ± 0.01 to 0.22 ± 0.04 Hz), the same silencing duration produces a nearly sixfold increase in the TKO slices (from 0.09 ± 0.02 to 0.5 ± 0.05 Hz; Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The same 2 days of TTX silencing produces a nearly sixfold increase in peak frequency in TKO slices (from 0.09 ± 0.02 to 0.5 ± 0.05 Hz).
source: While 2 days of TTX incubation increases the peak frequency 3.6-fold in wild-type (WT) slices (from 0.06 ± 0.01 to 0.22 ± 0.04 Hz), the same silencing duration produces a nearly sixfold increase in the TKO slices (from 0.09 ± 0.02 to 0.5 ± 0.05 Hz; Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A two-way ANOVA revealed significant effects of treatment (TTX vs. Control; p<0.0001) and genotype (p<0.0001) and a significant interaction between the two (p<0.0001) on peak frequency.
source: A two-way ANOVA revealed significant effects of treatment (TTX vs. Control; p<0.0001) and genotype (p<0.0001) and a significant interaction between the two (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: TTX increases in activity were highly significant in both WT (p=0.0007) and TKO (p<0.0001) slices.
source: Post hoc t tests (with Tukey correction for multiple comparisons) revealed that TTX increases in activity were highly significant in both WT (p=0.0007) and TKO (p<0.0001) slices and that TTX produced a significantly stronger increase in the TKO (p<0.0001), while the baseline activity of cells from slices derived from the TKO and WT do not differ significantly (p=0.92).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: TTX produced a significantly stronger increase in peak frequency in the TKO compared to WT (p<0.0001).
source: Post hoc t tests (with Tukey correction for multiple comparisons) revealed that TTX increases in activity were highly significant in both WT (p=0.0007) and TKO (p<0.0001) slices and that TTX produced a significantly stronger increase in the TKO (p<0.0001), while the baseline activity of cells from slices derived from the TKO and WT do not differ significantly (p=0.92).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: The baseline activity of cells from slices derived from the TKO and WT do not differ significantly (p=0.92).
source: Post hoc t tests (with Tukey correction for multiple comparisons) revealed that TTX increases in activity were highly significant in both WT (p=0.0007) and TKO (p<0.0001) slices and that TTX produced a significantly stronger increase in the TKO (p<0.0001), while the baseline activity of cells from slices derived from the TKO and WT do not differ significantly (p=0.92).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: The TTX condition increased synchrony from 0.76 ± 0.03 to 0.95 ± 0.01 in WT, and from 0.74 ± 0.03 to 0.94 ± 0.05 in the TKO.
source: The TTX condition also increased synchrony (from 0.76 ± 0.03 to 0.95 ± 0.01) in WT, and in the TKO (from 0.74 ± 0.03 to 0.94 ± 0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TTX effects on synchrony were highly significant (two-way ANOVA; p<0.0001), but there was no significant effect of genotype (p=0.43) and no interaction between treatment and genotype (p=0.65).
source: While the TTX effects were highly significant (two-way ANOVA; p<0.0001), there was no significant effect of genotype (p=0.43) and no interaction between treatment and genotype (p=0.65), presumably reflecting the fact that synchrony is already saturated by TTX treatment in the WT and cannot further increase in the TKO, but also indicating that baseline synchrony is not altered in the TKO.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: The PARbZIP family of TFs normally functions to restrain homeostatic plasticity, and in their absence, the homeostatic response is exaggerated.
source: These data suggest that the PARbZIP family of TFs normally functions to restrain homeostatic plasticity, and in their absence, the homeostatic response is exaggerated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing exaggerated responses in TKO mice.

claim: Even though the TKO mutation is associated with epilepsy, it does not make cortical neuronal circuits more excitable at baseline.
source: Moreover, even though the mutation is associated with epilepsy, it does not make cortical neuronal circuits more excitable at baseline.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing no difference in baseline activity between WT and TKO.

claim: In WT slices, activity deprivation causes hyperactivity, evident from a twofold rise in the peak frequency of the calcium activity.
source: In WT slices, activity deprivation causes hyperactivity, evident from a twofold rise in the peak frequency of the calcium activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: This exuberant activity in WT slices is restored back to baseline levels within 2 days following restoration of action potential firing.
source: However, this exuberant activity is restored back to baseline levels within 2 days following restoration of action potential firing.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the TKO slices, even though the initial response to TTX is exaggerated, the network is also able to return to baseline levels following 2 days of recovery, to levels indistinguishable from WT.
source: In the TKO slices, even though the initial response to TTX is exaggerated, the network is also able to return to baseline levels following 2 days of recovery, to levels indistinguishable from WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The recovery from a high activity state is not diminished in the TKO.
source: These data suggest that the recovery from a high activity state is not diminished in the TKO and suggest that the mutation in fact produces exaggerated homeostatic plasticity rather than a change in activity setpoint.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recovery data.

claim: The mutation produces exaggerated homeostatic plasticity rather than a change in activity setpoint.
source: These data suggest that the recovery from a high activity state is not diminished in the TKO and suggest that the mutation in fact produces exaggerated homeostatic plasticity rather than a change in activity setpoint.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recovery data.

claim: A robust upregulation of mEPSC amplitude following 2 days of activity deprivation was observed, consistent with homeostatic synaptic scaling.
source: We observed a robust upregulation of mEPSC amplitude following 2 days of activity deprivation, consistent with our understanding of homeostatic synaptic scaling (Turrigiano et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data and citation to prior literature.

claim: A large increase in mEPSC frequency was observed, which has been described in this preparation and in multiple other preparations.
source: We also observed a large increase in mEPSC frequency, which has also been described in this preparation (Koch et al., 2010) and in multiple other preparations (Wierenga et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data and citations to prior literature.

claim: In the TKO mice, the synaptic scaling is unaffected (amplitude increased from 13.4 ± 1.1 to 18.5 ± 1.2 pA in WT and from 13.2 ± 1.4 to 19.7 ± 1.1 pA in TKO).
source: In the TKO mice, the synaptic scaling is unaffected (Figure 3A and C; amplitude increased from 13.4 ± 1.1 to 18.5 ± 1.2 pA in WT and from 13.2 ± 1.4 to 19.7 ± 1.1 pA in TKO) but the increase in mEPSC frequency in response to activity deprivation is more dramatic (Figure 3B and D; 4.0 ± 0.8 to 6.2 ± 0.7 Hz in WT vs. 3.5 ± 0.5–9.3 ± 1.0 Hz in the KO).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The increase in mEPSC frequency in response to activity deprivation is more dramatic in TKO (4.0 ± 0.8 to 6.2 ± 0.7 Hz in WT vs. 3.5 ± 0.5–9.3 ± 1.0 Hz in the KO).
source: In the TKO mice, the synaptic scaling is unaffected (Figure 3A and C; amplitude increased from 13.4 ± 1.1 to 18.5 ± 1.2 pA in WT and from 13.2 ± 1.4 to 19.7 ± 1.1 pA in TKO) but the increase in mEPSC frequency in response to activity deprivation is more dramatic (Figure 3B and D; 4.0 ± 0.8 to 6.2 ± 0.7 Hz in WT vs. 3.5 ± 0.5–9.3 ± 1.0 Hz in the KO).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both the frequency and amplitude of mEPSCs are the same between WT and mutant slices at baseline.
source: Notably, both the frequency and amplitude of mEPSCs are the same between WT and mutant slices at baseline which parallels our observations of network activity (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The members of the PARbZIP family of TFs function to restrain upregulation of mEPSC frequency in response to activity deprivation and this increase is correlated with changes in activity levels across the network.
source: These results suggest that the members of the PARbZIP family of TFs function to restrain upregulation of mEPSC frequency in response to activity deprivation and this increase is correlated with changes in activity levels across the network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiology and calcium imaging data.

claim: In WT cultures, measurement of inhibitory input onto L5 pyramidal neurons revealed that both the amplitude and frequency of mIPSCs drop in response to activity deprivation.
source: In WT cultures, measurement of inhibitory input onto L5 pyramidal neurons revealed that both the amplitude and frequency of mIPSCs drop in response to activity deprivation (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In TKO slices, a similar decrease in mIPSC frequency following 48 hr TTX treatment was observed, although the amplitude of the change was smaller than in the WT.
source: When we measured mIPSCs in pyramidal neurons from TKO slices, we saw a similar decrease in frequency following 48 hr TTX treatment, although the amplitude of the change was smaller than in the WT (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mIPSC amplitude change is abolished in TKO: mIPSC amplitude is decreased at baseline compared to WT but did not show a further decrease after TTX treatment.
source: In contrast, the mIPSC amplitude change is abolished: mIPSC amplitude is decreased at baseline compared to WT but did not show a further decrease after TTX treatment (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The decreased mIPSC amplitude at baseline does not correlate with the unchanged baseline network activity levels.
source: However, the decreased amplitude in the untreated condition does not correlate with the unchanged baseline network activity levels (Figure 2), suggesting that the decrease of mIPSCs amplitude at baseline may be insufficient on its own to cause network hyperexcitability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the mIPSC data with the network activity data.

claim: Both the amplitude and frequency of mIPSCs received by pyramidal neurons after activity deprivation are indistinguishable from the WT in the TKO slices.
source: Thus, both the amplitude and frequency of mIPSCs received by pyramidal neurons after activity deprivation are indistinguishable from the WT in the TKO slices, suggesting that homeostatic plasticity of mIPSCs is not directly driving the changes in the network activity following TTX treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mIPSC data.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity of mIPSCs is not directly driving the changes in the network activity following TTX treatment.
source: Thus, both the amplitude and frequency of mIPSCs received by pyramidal neurons after activity deprivation are indistinguishable from the WT in the TKO slices, suggesting that homeostatic plasticity of mIPSCs is not directly driving the changes in the network activity following TTX treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mIPSC data.

claim: Changes in neuronal excitability have been described as part of the homeostatic response to activity deprivation.
source: Changes in neuronal excitability have also been described as part of the homeostatic response to activity deprivation (Desai et al., 1999; Karmarkar and Buonomano, 2006; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013; Moore et al., 2018; Yoshimura and Rasband, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: WT L5 pyramidal neurons become more excitable following prolonged activity deprivation.
source: WT L5 pyramidal neurons become more excitable following prolonged activity deprivation (Figure 5; Desai et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5 and citation to prior literature.

claim: Changes in excitability due to activity deprivation are accompanied by a shift in the average adaptation ratio of the cells in both WT and TKO slices (control WT: 3.8 ± 0.16, TTX WT: 0.72 ± 0.22, TKO control: 0.46 ± 0.25, TKO TTX: 0.71 ± 0.33).
source: Changes in excitability due to activity deprivation are accompanied by a shift in the average adaptation ratio of the cells in both WT and TKO slices (control WT: 3.8 ± 0.16, TTX WT: 0.72 ± 0.22, TKO control: 0.46 ± 0.25, TKO TTX: 0.71 ± 0.33; two-way ANOVA significant difference between control and TTX and no significant difference between WT and TKO).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data with statistical analysis.

claim: Excitatory neurons in L5 in the slices prepared from TKO animals are equally excitable at baseline and also show upregulation of intrinsic excitability to the same extent as WT.
source: Excitatory neurons in L5 in the slices prepared from TKO animals are equally excitable at baseline and also show upregulation of intrinsic excitability to the same extent (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Changes in intrinsic excitability are not driving the exaggerated network response to activity deprivation and this form of homeostatic plasticity is not under the control of the Par bZIP TF family.
source: These results suggest that changes in intrinsic excitability are not driving the exaggerated network response to activity deprivation and this form of homeostatic plasticity is not under the control of the Par bZIP TF family.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the intrinsic excitability data.

claim: All three Par bZIP family members form homo- and heterodimers and bind to the same PAR-response element.
source: Because all three Par bZIP family members form homo- and heterodimers and bind to the same PAR-response element (Gachon, 2007), they may be able to compensate for one another.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The model with the highest adjusted R2 was that which depended only on the sum of the number of Hlf and Tef alleles.
source: Since the model with the highest adjusted R2 was that which depended only on the sum of the number of Hlf and Tef alleles (line 6), we used this model for further post hoc (Tukey) tests to determine the effect of different numbers of alleles on the TTX response.
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate linear modeling analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The most significant differences in TTX response were between TKO slices (0 alleles; n = 32, mean = 0.48) and the other genotypes tested (1 allele, n = 16, mean = 0.32; 2 alleles, n = 26, mean = 0.35; and 4 alleles, n = 24, mean = 0.23; p < 0.0001–0.0014).
source: The most significant differences were between TKO slices (0 alleles; n = 32, mean = 0.48) and the other genotypes tested (1 allele, n = 16, mean = 0.32; 2 alleles, n = 26, mean = 0.35; and 4 alleles, n = 24, mean = 0.23; p < 0.0001–0.0014).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data across genotypes.

claim: Most of the difference between TKO (0 alleles of Hlf + Tef) and WT (4 alleles of Hlf + Tef) could be restored by a single allele.
source: This indicates that most of the difference between TKO (0 alleles of Hlf + Tef) and WT (4 alleles of Hlf + Tef) could be restored by a single allele, although there was a small but significant improvement between two and four alleles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of calcium imaging data across genotypes.

claim: There was a small but significant improvement in TTX response between two and four alleles of Hlf + Tef.
source: This indicates that most of the difference between TKO (0 alleles of Hlf + Tef) and WT (4 alleles of Hlf + Tef) could be restored by a single allele, although there was a small but significant improvement between two and four alleles.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing a significant difference between WT and 2 allele responses (p = 0.011).

claim: A separate analysis of variance of three subgroups with two alleles (WT for Hlf but lacking Tef, WT for Tef and lacking Hlf, and trans-Het heterozygous for both) revealed that the means (0.32, 0.41, and 0.33) were not significantly different (p = 0.28).
source: A separate analysis of variance of these three subgroups revealed that the means (0.32, 0.41, and 0.33) were not significantly different (p = 0.28), consistent with the hypothesis that alleles of Hlf and Tef can substitute for one another in their ability to regulate the homeostatic response to activity deprivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: Alleles of Hlf and Tef can substitute for one another in their ability to regulate the homeostatic response to activity deprivation.
source: A separate analysis of variance of these three subgroups revealed that the means (0.32, 0.41, and 0.33) were not significantly different (p = 0.28), consistent with the hypothesis that alleles of Hlf and Tef can substitute for one another in their ability to regulate the homeostatic response to activity deprivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis showing no difference between different combinations of Hlf and Tef alleles totaling two.

claim: TKO animals develop spontaneous seizures and have a dramatically decreased lifespan.
source: TKO animals develop spontaneous seizures and have a dramatically decreased lifespan (Gachon et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and by observations in the current study.

claim: Just one allele of either Hlf or Tef restores the lifespan of the animals to levels not statistically different from WT.
source: However, just one allele of either Hlf or Tef restores the lifespan of the animals to levels not statistically different from WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mice with one Dbp allele have improved survival compared to TKO animals but still die at a statistically significant higher rate than WT mice.
source: Mice with one Dbp allele have improved survival compared to TKO animals but still die at a statistically significant higher rate than WT mice (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Even though Dbp is dispensable for restraining homeostatic plasticity in the cortex, it may play a role in preventing premature death by functioning elsewhere in the brain or peripheral tissue.
source: These results differ from the cortical network activity response to activity deprivation in organotypic slices where the presence of Dbp had no effect on the constraint of homeostatic plasticity. This suggests that even though Dbp is dispensable for restraining homeostatic plasticity in the cortex, it may play a role in preventing premature death by functioning elsewhere in the brain or peripheral tissue (Stewart et al., 2020) since these TFs are expressed and play important roles there (Wahlestedt et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the cortical slice data with the survival data, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A single allele of Hlf and Tef is enough to compensate for loss of the rest of the family members and restore survival to WT levels.
source: However, a single allele of Hlf and Tef is enough to compensate for loss of the rest of the family members and restore survival to WT levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Inappropriately triggered homeostatic plasticity can either fail to compensate for changes in activity or can itself destabilize network activity.
source: Inappropriately triggered homeostatic plasticity can either fail to compensate for changes in activity or can itself destabilize network activity (Nelson and Valakh, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Reduced activity, which initiates a compensatory increase in network excitability, also activates a set of TFs that function to restrain homeostasis.
source: Here, we show that reduced activity, which initiates a compensatory increase in network excitability, also activates a set of TFs that function to restrain homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity is negatively regulated through the PARbZIP family of TFs.
source: Thus, we propose a model in which homeostatic plasticity is negatively regulated through the PARbZIP family of TFs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Excitatory neurons respond to a global drop in network activity by upregulating the frequency and amplitude of excitatory synaptic currents, decreasing inhibitory currents, and increasing intrinsic excitability.
source: Excitatory neurons respond to a global drop in network activity by upregulating the frequency and amplitude of excitatory synaptic currents, decreasing inhibitory currents, and increasing intrinsic excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: These changes correlate with dramatically increased network activity immediately following removal of activity blockade that 'overshoots' initial activity levels.
source: These changes correlate with dramatically increased network activity immediately following removal of activity blockade that 'overshoots' initial activity levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Synaptic scaling of excitatory synapses has previously been shown to depend on intact transcription and translation.
source: Synaptic scaling of excitatory synapses has previously been shown to depend on intact transcription and translation (Dörrbaum et al., 2020; Goold and Nicoll, 2010; Ibata et al., 2008; Schanzenbächer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of Hlf, Tef, and Dbp results in exaggerated homeostatic changes.
source: Here, we demonstrate a second role for transcription in regulating the strength of the network homeostatic response. Loss of Hlf, Tef, and Dbp results in exaggerated homeostatic changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing exaggerated responses in TKO mice.

claim: The levels of network activity at baseline are unchanged in TKO mice.
source: However, the levels of network activity at baseline are unchanged.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing no difference in baseline activity.

claim: These TFs are activated to restrain homeostatic signaling rather than downregulating network dynamics directly.
source: This suggests that these TFs are activated to restrain homeostatic signaling rather than downregulating network dynamics directly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that baseline activity is unchanged but homeostatic responses are exaggerated in TKO mice.

claim: This is the first negative regulator of homeostasis to be described.
source: While a few other genes have been described that have limited effects on network dynamics, but are required for homeostatic plasticity (Shank3, Tatavarty et al., 2020; FMRP, Soden and Chen, 2010; and Caspr2, Fernandes et al., 2019), this is, to our knowledge, the first negative regulator of homeostasis to be described.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior literature and the novelty of the current findings.

claim: Present data implicate mEPSC frequency, but not amplitude, as the site of the restraint of homeostatic plasticity.
source: Present data implicate mEPSC frequency, but not amplitude, as the site of the restraint of homeostatic plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiology data showing differential effects on mEPSC frequency vs. amplitude in TKO mice.

claim: Although 2 days of activity blockade in dissociated cortical cultures were initially found to produce scaling up of EPSC amplitudes without accompanying changes in mEPSC frequency, multiple subsequent studies have found evidence for changes in both amplitude and frequency.
source: Although 2 days of activity blockade in dissociated cortical cultures were initially found to produce scaling up of EPSC amplitudes without accompanying changes in mEPSC frequency (Turrigiano et al., 1998), multiple subsequent studies have found evidence for changes in both amplitude and frequency as found here (Echegoyen et al., 2007; Koch et al., 2010; Thiagarajan et al., 2005; Wierenga et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Changes in mini frequency are typically interpreted as reflecting increased presynaptic release, either via increases in the numbers of synapses or active release sites, or via changes in the rate at which spontaneous, action potential independent release occurs at each site.
source: Changes in mini frequency are typically interpreted as reflecting increased presynaptic release, either via increases in the numbers of synapses or active release sites, or via changes in the rate at which spontaneous, action potential independent release occurs at each site.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The increase observed in mEPSC frequency (1.7-fold greater in TKO than WT) was lower than the relative increase in activity levels measured from the frequency of calcium transients (2.5-fold greater in TKO than WT at 5 days).
source: Although the increase observed in mEPSC frequency (1.7-fold greater in TKO than WT), was lower than the relative increase in activity levels, measured from the frequency of calcium transients (2.5-fold greater in TKO than WT at 5 days), these two measures need not be linearly related.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Mini frequency can be distinct from action potential evoked release.
source: First, mini frequency can be distinct from action potential evoked release (Crawford et al., 2017), and second, in a highly recurrent network, the relationship between firing and synaptic strength can be nonlinear (Toyoizumi and Abbott, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In a highly recurrent network, the relationship between firing and synaptic strength can be nonlinear.
source: First, mini frequency can be distinct from action potential evoked release (Crawford et al., 2017), and second, in a highly recurrent network, the relationship between firing and synaptic strength can be nonlinear (Toyoizumi and Abbott, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Hlf and Tef are expressed in inhibitory neurons and are also upregulated by inactivity.
source: We cannot eliminate the contribution of inhibitory neurons as a contributing factor to homeostatic plasticity restraint, since Hlf and Tef are expressed in this neuronal type and are also upregulated by inactivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: mIPSCs received by excitatory neurons cannot explain the exaggerated network hyperexcitability caused by TTX incubation in TKO slices since neither the amplitude nor frequency of mIPSCs is different in the TTX condition.
source: mIPSCs received by excitatory neurons cannot explain the exaggerated network hyperexcitability caused by TTX incubation in TKO slices since neither the amplitude nor frequency of mIPSCs is different in the TTX condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mIPSC data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The amplitude of mIPSCs is decreased at baseline in the untreated TKO cultures.
source: We note, however, that the amplitude of mIPSCs is decreased at baseline in the untreated cultures.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The decrease of mIPSCs amplitude at baseline is insufficient on its own to induce network excitability, since baseline network activity was unchanged in the TKO.
source: Such decrease of the strength of inhibitory currents is insufficient on its own to induce network excitability, since baseline network activity was unchanged in the TKO, but it may make the network more vulnerable to future insults.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the mIPSC data with the network activity data.

claim: The decreased baseline mIPSC amplitude may make the network more vulnerable to future insults.
source: Such decrease of the strength of inhibitory currents is insufficient on its own to induce network excitability, since baseline network activity was unchanged in the TKO, but it may make the network more vulnerable to future insults.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential consequences of the decreased mIPSC amplitude.

claim: Partial genetic compensation of DBP for the survival phenotype but not the homeostatic plasticity phenotype suggests that the propensity to develop seizures and diminished survival have a more complex origin involving other brain regions and perhaps other organs of the body.
source: However, partial genetic compensation of DBP for the survival phenotype but not the homeostatic plasticity phenotype as assayed by calcium imaging, suggests that the propensity to develop seizures and diminished survival have a more complex origin involving other brain regions and perhaps other organs of the body.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the cortical slice data with the survival data.

claim: Gachon et al., 2004 first reported that deletion of the PARbZIP proteins TEF, HLF, and DBP caused spontaneous and audiogenic seizures.
source: Gachon et al., 2004 first reported that deletion of the PARbZIP proteins TEF, HLF, and DBP caused spontaneous and audiogenic seizures.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Gachon et al., 2004 suggested that seizures in TKO mice may reflect effects on neurotransmitter metabolism caused by a reduction in pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) since pyridoxal kinase, which catalyzes the last step in the conversion of vitamin B6 into PLP is a target of the PARbZIP proteins.
source: They suggested that this may reflect effects on neurotransmitter metabolism caused by a reduction in pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) since pyridoxal kinase, which catalyzes the last step in the conversion of vitamin B6 into PLP is a target of the PARbZIP proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Using HPLC, Gachon et al., 2004 found no changes in GABA or glutamate, but reduced levels of dopamine, serotonin, and histamine in the knockout animals.
source: Using HPLC, they found no changes in GABA or glutamate, but reduced levels of dopamine, serotonin, and histamine in the knockout animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Changes in amine transmitters are unlikely to contribute to plasticity in cortical slice cultures which do not include the brainstem nuclei from which these projections arise.
source: Although changes in amine transmitters could potentially contribute to phenotypes in vivo, they are unlikely to contribute to plasticity in cortical slice cultures which do not include the brainstem nuclei from which these projections arise.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from knowledge about the anatomy of the slice culture preparation.

claim: Reduced glutamate decarboxylase action could potentially have contributed to the observed baseline reduction in mIPSCs since heterozygous and homozygous mutants of Gad1 have reduced mIPSC amplitudes.
source: Reduced glutamate decarboxylase action could potentially have contributed to the observed baseline reduction in mIPSCs since heterozygous (Lazarus et al., 2015) and homozygous (Lau and Murthy, 2012) mutants of Gad1, the gene encoding the GAD67 isoform of glutamic acid decarboxylase, have reduced mIPSC amplitudes.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Reduced glutamate decarboxylase action does not account for the enhanced homeostatic overshoot following activity blockade, since in the TKO animals, activity blockade did not produce any further reduction in inhibition, but produced robust changes at excitatory synapses.
source: However, this does not account for the enhanced homeostatic overshoot following activity blockade, since in the TKO animals, activity blockade did not produce any further reduction in inhibition, but produced robust changes at excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiology data.

claim: HLF and TEF form homo- or heterodimers and recognize similar DNA sequences.
source: HLF and TEF form homo- or heterodimers and recognize similar DNA sequences (Gachon, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: These TFs can powerfully compensate for the loss of other family members.
source: Here, we demonstrate that these TFs can powerfully compensate for the loss of other family members.
evidence: This claim is supported by the genetic analysis data shown in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: The peak frequency of calcium transients depends roughly equally on Hlf and Tef but does not appear to depend on Dbp.
source: We varied genotype for all three PARbZip factors and used multiple regression models to show that the peak frequency of calcium transients depends roughly equally on Hlf and Tef but does not appear to depend on Dbp.
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate linear modeling analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: A single allele of either Hlf or Tef in the complete absence of the other factors is sufficient to preserve the normal restraint of homeostatic plasticity, producing a response to activity deprivation that is not significantly different from WT.
source: It also appears that a single allele of either Hlf or Tef in the complete absence of the other factors is sufficient to preserve the normal restraint of homeostatic plasticity, producing a response to activity deprivation that is not significantly different from WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data across genotypes.

claim: Tef and Hlf can robustly compensate for loss of each other and completely restore life span.
source: We also found, in agreement with prior findings (Gachon et al., 2004), that Tef and Hlf can robustly compensate for loss of each other and completely restore life span.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 7 and citation to prior literature.

claim: Such robust compensation and functional redundancy of these TFs highlight their importance and may explain why they have not been identified in GWAS studies as risk factors for epilepsy or other neuropsychiatric diseases.
source: Such robust compensation and functional redundancy of these TFs highlight their importance and may explain why they have not been identified in GWAS studies as risk factors for epilepsy or other neuropsychiatric diseases.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the functional redundancy.

claim: The mechanisms linking activity deprivation to Tef and Hlf activation seem likely to depend on reduced calcium influx.
source: The mechanisms linking activity deprivation to Tef and Hlf activation were not directly addressed in this work, but seem likely to depend on reduced calcium influx.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanisms.

claim: Prior studies have suggested alternately that scaling up of mEPSC amplitudes depends upon calcium influx through either T-type or L-type calcium channels.
source: Prior studies have suggested alternately that scaling up of mEPSC amplitudes depends upon calcium influx through either T-type (Schaukowitch et al., 2017) or L-type (Li et al., 2020) calcium channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The T-type calcium channel pathway has been found to depend on the activity-dependent TFs ELK1 and SRF.
source: The former pathway has also been found to depend on the activity-dependent TFs ELK1 and SRF.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature (Schaukowitch et al., 2017).

claim: Activation of the constraining TFs Tef and Hlf could be secondary or delayed responses dependent on changes in the transcription and translation of other activity-dependent TFs, or may represent a primary response to activity deprivation.
source: Activation of the constraining TFs Tef and Hlf could be secondary or delayed responses dependent on changes in the transcription and translation of other activity-dependent TFs, or may represent a primary response to activity deprivation, analogous to, but in the opposite direction of the well-studied immediate early genes such as Fos, Arc, and others.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanisms of Tef and Hlf activation.

claim: Besides their function in early embryonic development, the PARbZip TFs have been extensively studied for their roles in circadian rhythms in flies, zebrafish, and rodents.
source: Besides their function in early embryonic development (Gavriouchkina et al., 2010; Wahlestedt et al., 2017), the PARbZip TFs have been extensively studied for their roles in circadian rhythms in flies, zebrafish, and rodents (Cyran et al., 2003; Vatine et al., 2009; Weger et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The present finding that Hlf and Tef act to restrain homeostatic plasticity is consistent with a recent report demonstrating that PARbZIP TFs are differentially expressed in human epileptogenic tissue.
source: The present finding that Hlf and Tef also act to restrain homeostatic plasticity is consistent with a recent report demonstrating that PARbZIP TFs are differentially expressed in human epileptogenic tissue (Rambousek et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: CLOCK, an upstream regulator of PARbZIP TFs, is necessary in cortical excitatory neurons for maintaining normal network activity and leads to epilepsy when conditionally deleted in these neurons.
source: In addition, CLOCK, an upstream regulator of these TFs, is necessary in cortical excitatory neurons for maintaining normal network activity and leads to epilepsy when conditionally deleted in these neurons (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Multiple components of the molecular clock are robustly expressed in the neocortex, consistent with the idea that they might have an additional function in the cortex that is distinct from their circadian role in SCN.
source: Multiple components of the molecular clock are robustly expressed in the neocortex (Bering et al., 2018; Gachon et al., 2004; Kobayashi et al., 2015), consistent with the idea that they might have an additional function in the cortex that is distinct from their circadian role in SCN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents an inference about the function of clock genes in cortex.

claim: The role of core clock genes in homeostatic plasticity has not yet been explored.
source: However, the role of core clock genes in homeostatic plasticity has not yet been explored.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: During the first few weeks of postnatal development in rodents, cortical neurons go from receiving few synapses to receiving thousands.
source: During the first few weeks of postnatal development in rodents, cortical neurons go from receiving few synapses to receiving thousands.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cortical development.

claim: The large increase in synapses during development may require developmental downregulation of the strength of homeostatic plasticity.
source: This may require developmental downregulation of the strength of homeostatic plasticity.
evidence: This is speculation about the developmental role of homeostatic plasticity regulation.

claim: Neuropsychiatric diseases, such as monogenic causes of ASD, can trigger homeostatic changes in circuit properties which restore overall firing rates, but nonetheless have maladaptive effects on cortical function and flexibility.
source: Neuropsychiatric diseases, such as monogenic causes of ASD, can trigger homeostatic changes in circuit properties which restore overall firing rates, but nonetheless have maladaptive effects on cortical function and flexibility (Antoine et al., 2019; Nelson and Valakh, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of function of genes giving rise to developmental disorders can cause failures of homeostatic plasticity.
source: Conversely, loss of function of genes giving rise to developmental disorders can cause failures of homeostatic plasticity (Blackman et al., 2012; Genç et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: These findings provide a potential target for enhancing homeostatic plasticity in contexts where it is insufficient, or for downregulating it when it is maladaptive.
source: Our findings provide a potential target for enhancing homeostatic plasticity in contexts where it is insufficient, or for downregulating it when it is maladaptive, and therefore provide an avenue for identifying how the positive and negative regulators of homeostasis interact to stabilize network activity.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential therapeutic implications of the findings.
